title: The Foam Company Quietly Printing Record Profits: UFP Technologies
description: A $2.5 billion medical device contract manufacturer just posted record earnings and beat estimates by double digits, sending shares up over 11% -- and almost nobody noticed. Alex and Jordan dig into UFP Technologies, the unglamorous foam-and-plastics company quietly powering hospital supply chains, and explain why this steady compounder still flies under Wall Street's radar.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: So I want to start with a number that should grab your attention even if you've never heard this company's name before: a stock that jumped over eleven percent in premarket trading off an earnings report, and almost nobody outside of a few analyst desks even noticed it happened.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Eleven percent on an earnings pop is not a small move. That's the kind of thing that usually leads financial Twitter for a day.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Right, except this one barely got a mention anywhere, because the company is called UFP Technologies, ticker UFPT, and it makes foam and plastic components for medical devices. It's about as unsexy a business description as you'll hear on this show.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Unsexy is kind of our whole brand at this point. But I'll say, a company that can put up a stock move like that on earnings and still stay quiet is exactly the kind of thing worth twenty minutes of anyone's time, because either the market's about to catch up to it, or there's a real reason it's been ignored.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: That's the tension we're going to sit in today. This is a genuinely small, genuinely under-covered company, about two and a half billion dollars in market cap, and it just posted record earnings. So let's figure out what it actually does, because the name alone won't tell you much.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Okay, so here's the plain-English version. UFP Technologies is what's called a contract development and manufacturing organization, or CDMO, but specifically for single-use and single-patient medical devices.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Think about everything in a hospital that gets used once and thrown away, or used for exactly one patient and then discarded for safety reasons. Surgical positioning pads, wound care components, specialized foam and plastic parts that go inside or around actual devices. Big medical device companies need those parts made precisely and made reliably, but they don't necessarily want to build and staff a factory to do it themselves.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: So UFP is basically the behind-the-scenes manufacturer that the household-name device companies quietly rely on.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Exactly that. And the revenue model is built on long-term customer relationships and program-based contracts, so once they're designed into a device or a supply chain, they tend to stay there for years. That's a sticky, recurring kind of revenue, which is a nice foundation for a business.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: And it's not purely organic growth either. They've got an active acquisition strategy, folding in smaller, adjacent companies to add capacity or new capabilities. One example in the notes is a unit called AJR, which they've been expanding to help fuel some of this recent growth.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Right, so you've got two growth engines running at once: the base business growing mid-to-high single digits organically, and then bolt-on M&A layered on top pushing total growth into the low-double-digit to high-teens range over time. That combination is worth remembering because it shows up directly in the numbers we're about to go through.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Which brings us to the actual earnings, because this is where it gets fun. Let's start with the most recent quarter, Q2 2026, reported early August.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Revenue came in at $173.96 million, up 15.1 percent year over year. Organic sales growth alone was 12.4 percent, and management was explicit that this was broad-based demand across their whole MedTech platform, not one hot program or one big customer carrying the quarter.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Adjusted EPS was $2.92, up 16.8 percent year over year, and that's a record for the company. Gross margin ticked up too, from 28.8 percent to 29.3 percent. And here's the kicker: they beat Wall Street's adjusted EPS estimate by roughly 23 percent, and the revenue estimate by about 9 percent. That's not a small beat, that's a blowout.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: A 23 percent EPS beat is genuinely rare for a company this size that isn't some speculative growth story. That's the kind of number that usually means analysts had the model wrong in a meaningful way, not just a rounding difference.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: And the stock reacted exactly like you'd expect, jumping over eleven percent in premarket on the news. Management flagged something interesting looking ahead too: they mentioned an 'eight-figure' new contribution heading into 2027, though they were careful not to give explicit guidance for the rest of this year. They just reiterated their long-term organic growth target of roughly six to nine percent.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: That eight-figure comment is intriguing without being a lot of detail. It sounds like a new program or contract win that's material enough to call out on the call, but not fully quantified yet. That's the kind of thing that tends to become clearer in future quarters.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Now here's where the story gets more interesting, because Q2 wasn't always going to look like this. If you rewind to Q1 2026, reported back in May, the picture was a lot murkier.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Right, Q1 was the softer quarter. Net sales were $154.2 million, up 4.1 percent from $148.1 million a year earlier. Net income was $17.5 million, up just 1.8 percent year over year. GAAP EPS was $2.24, adjusted EPS was $2.48.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Compare that four percent revenue growth to the fifteen percent we just talked about in Q2, and you can see why investors got nervous. There was also active M&A commentary around that release, which added some uncertainty about where the growth was actually coming from. The stock had already had a rough ninety-day stretch heading into that report, down mid-teens percent, and while there was a decent rebound right after Q1 earnings, the bigger question of whether growth was actually going to reaccelerate was still hanging out there.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: So basically the market was pricing in real doubt about this company's growth trajectory, and then Q2 came along and just answered that doubt directly.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: That's exactly the arc here. You had a stock that fell sharply on growth-slowdown fears, and then the very next quarter delivered double-digit organic growth, a record adjusted EPS, and margin expansion on top of it. That's about as clean a myth-busting quarter as you'll see.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: And the price action tells that story too. Shares snapped back nearly 20 percent over just seven days after the Q2 report, and were up around 15 percent over the trailing 30 days. That's the market rapidly re-rating the stock once the fear turned out to be overblown.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Which is a pretty useful lesson in itself. Sometimes a stock selling off hard isn't a red flag about the business, it's just the market extrapolating one slow quarter further than it should have.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Let's talk about what's been happening more recently outside of the earnings reports, because there's been a decent amount of news flow even if most of it hasn't made headlines. The company's been on the investor conference circuit lately, showing up at both the Midwest IDEAS and East Coast IDEAS conferences.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: At those, management reiterated a targeted growth algorithm of twelve to eighteen percent annually, combining organic growth with acquisitions, and they kept emphasizing global MedTech expansion as a theme. That's consistent with everything we just walked through in the earnings, but it's worth noting they're saying the same thing to a room of investors that they're saying on the earnings call, which is a good sign of consistency.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: And around the Q1 release specifically, there was commentary about an active but 'disciplined' M&A pipeline. That word disciplined is doing some work there. It suggests they're not just buying anything that moves to pad growth, they're being selective about bolt-on deals that add real capacity or capabilities.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Which fits their whole historical playbook. This is a company built on folding in niche device-component makers over time rather than making one giant transformative acquisition. It's a slow, compounding strategy rather than a headline-grabbing one.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: That's actually a big part of why this company doesn't get much attention, and it's worth spelling out explicitly since that's the whole premise of the show. There's no single flashy product here, no drug trial readout, no viral consumer brand. It's a contract manufacturer of things like foam positioning pads and wound care components, which is about as far from a hype cycle as healthcare gets.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: And at roughly two and a half billion in market cap, it's genuinely small and mid-cap. It's not the kind of name that shows up in a typical retail investor's portfolio or gets casually mentioned on financial television. The story here is steady execution and disciplined tuck-in M&A, not a single dramatic narrative that pulls in coverage.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: But that's also exactly why the numbers we just went through matter so much. A record adjusted EPS, mid-teens revenue growth, expanding gross margins, and a double-digit earnings beat, all happening quietly while the company operates in a corner of healthcare most people never think about.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: So what would actually change that and pull this thing into the spotlight? A few things stand out. More outsized earnings beats like this last one would obviously help, since that's what generated the media attention it did get, even if it was limited.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: A larger, more visible acquisition could do it too, something bigger than the usual bolt-on that gets analysts and press paying closer attention. And there's a broader macro angle here as well, with the whole reshoring and onshoring of device manufacturing theme, plus the general growth of single-use devices in healthcare. If that narrative gets more attention on Wall Street, a company like this sits right in the middle of it.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: It's kind of the classic under-the-radar setup: solid fundamentals, a boring-sounding business, and a catalyst that hasn't quite arrived yet to force broader coverage.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Which is exactly why we think it's worth flagging now rather than after that catalyst shows up. If the growth algorithm they've laid out actually holds, twelve to eighteen percent annually between organic growth and M&A, that's a pretty compelling long-term compounding story hiding in plain sight.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: Before we wrap up, we do need to say the obligatory but genuinely important part.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Quick reminder before we get into it: everything in this episode is for informational and entertainment purposes only. It is not financial advice, and you should always do your own research or talk to a licensed financial advisor before making investment decisions.

lines.speaker: alex
lines.text: So that's UFP Technologies for you, the foam and plastics company nobody's talking about that just quietly put up a record quarter.

lines.speaker: jordan
lines.text: Thanks for spending this time with us. We'll catch you next episode with another name that deserves more attention than it's getting.
